So you are eleven, and you already know where you want to go. That is earlier than most people who write to me.
I know. My neighbour David wants the same university, so we talk about it a lot.
Good. Tell me something first: if you got a place there, what would you actually do in the first year?
I would major in law. After that I would train as a pilot in France.
That is a real answer, and most people your age give me a feeling instead. Now the harder question. What do you do that nobody makes you do?
I make cakes and I sell them at the market in our condominium, every two weeks. I keep the money in my own account.
Then that is extracurricular, and it is worth more than you think. Half the applicants I read have never run anything.
I thought admissions only looked at grades and at the essay.
Grades get your file opened. After that we are reading for a person. If everybody in the pile has perfect grades, grades cannot make anybody stand out.
And if I could only fix one thing before I apply, what would you tell me to fix?
Your writing, and not your English. Slow down and read your own sentences out loud before you send them. If I were you, I would start that habit now and not at seventeen.
If I were you, I would read the essay out loud before sending it.
Thousands of applicants have perfect grades, so grades alone do not make you stand out.
The essay is the only part of the application that sounds like you.

People ask me what we look for, and they always expect a number. The truth is that the grades only get your file opened. After that, we are reading for something else. We want to know what you did when nobody was making you do it. A boy last year ran a small business at a street market with his neighbour, and he wrote about the week he lost money. That page told me more than any test score. So do not send us a list of everything you have ever won. Send us one thing you actually built, and tell us what it cost you.

I am in my second year here, and I came from Sao Paulo. If somebody had told me at eleven that I would be sitting in this library, I would have laughed. The hardest part was not the English. It was learning to write slowly. At home I answered fast, because answering fast was how you looked clever. Here nobody is impressed by fast. They read what you wrote, and they ask you why you chose that word and not another one. If I could go back and change one habit, I would read my own sentences out loud before sending them. That single thing would have saved me a whole term.

My name is Gabriel and I am eleven years old. I want to study in the United States, and I have wanted that for a long time. If I got a place at a university like that, I would study law first. After my degree, I would train as a pilot in France. That is the plan, and I am starting with my English.
